# Hand Lettering

The sign above Dot's Diner had been fading for eleven years, and nobody had noticed until Dot died.

Then everyone noticed at once. Walking past on the way to the funeral home, people looked up and saw what the weather had done: the red of *DOT'S* gone the color of a healed scar, the apostrophe entirely lost, so that the sign now read DOTS DINER, like a place that served punctuation.

Walt Kessler noticed from his kitchen window across the street, where he had been noticing things for most of his seventy-nine years. He had painted that sign in 1974. He remembered the day because Dot had paid him partly in cash and partly in pie, and he had argued with her about the ratio, and she had won.

He called her son.

"I'd like to repaint the sign," he said. "Before Saturday."

There was a pause on the line, the kind of pause that is really a man deciding whether to explain something. "Mr. Kessler, we're selling the building. Somebody's turning it into a vape place, I think. Or a phone store."

"I know."

"So the sign's coming down in a month anyway."

"I know," Walt said. "I'd still like to repaint it."

---

His hands were the problem. They had been the problem for a while. A sign painter's hand is supposed to be a steady thing, a tool that happens to be attached to a person, and Walt's had started to feel more like a person attached to a tool: opinionated, easily tired, occasionally trembling in a way that had nothing to do with fear.

He went to the garage and found his kit. The brushes were still good. He had cared for them the way some men care for guns. The quill of a lettering brush, long and soft, has to be cleaned in oil and shaped with the fingers and stored flat, and he had done all that for decades after anyone was paying him to. He unrolled the canvas wrap and there they were, laid out like a set of surgical instruments for an operation nobody performed anymore.

The paint was harder. One-Shot enamel had changed its formula since he'd last bought any, and the man at the hardware store, a boy really, had to look it up on a tablet. Walt stood at the counter feeling like a visitor from a country that had been dissolved.

---

Thursday morning, he set up the ladder.

A few people stopped to watch, which he'd expected. What he hadn't expected was that they'd stay. A woman with a stroller. Two teenagers who were supposed to be somewhere else. The man from the bank. Nobody said much. They stood the way people stand around a campfire, a little hypnotized by something happening slowly.

He started with the D.

There's a secret to hand lettering that he had tried to explain to his apprentices back when he had them: you don't paint the letter. You paint the stroke, and the letter emerges. A capital D is two decisions, a vertical and a curve, and the curve is where most people fail, because they try to draw it. You can't draw a good curve. You have to commit to it, load the brush, turn your wrist, and pull, trusting that your body remembers what your mind has forgotten.

His hand shook at the top of the curve. He stopped, lowered the brush, breathed.

"You okay up there?" called the man from the bank.

"Fine," said Walt, which was a lie, and then he loaded the brush again and made the curve, and it was not perfect but it was good, and it was his.

---

By noon he had DOT on the board, and his shoulders felt like someone had filled them with wet sand.

The woman with the stroller had gone and come back with a coffee, which she handed up to him without asking how he took it. Black. She'd guessed right. He wondered if he looked like a man who took his coffee black, and decided he probably did.

"Did you know her?" she asked.

"Fifty years," he said.

"Were you—" She didn't finish.

"No," Walt said. "Nothing like that. She was married to Frank, and I was married to Ellen, and then they were gone, and we were two old people who ate breakfast in the same place. She was my friend."

He didn't say the rest of it: that for the past six years, since Ellen, Dot's had been the only place he went where anyone expected him. That she kept his mug, an ugly brown one, on a hook behind the counter. That when he'd missed two mornings in a row last winter with the flu, she had shown up at his door with soup and a lecture, and he had been so happy to be scolded that he'd nearly cried.

---

He saved the apostrophe for last.

It was the smallest mark on the sign and the one that mattered. Without it, DOTS was just a word. With it, it was a person, a possession, a claim. *This belongs to someone.* He loaded the tip of the brush with the barest amount of red, touched it to the board, and flicked it down into a small tapered comma floating in the air.

When he climbed down, his knees objecting at every rung, there were maybe fifteen people on the sidewalk. Somebody started clapping, and then felt embarrassed about it, and stopped, and then somebody else started, and they all joined in, and Walt stood there holding his brush like a man who'd been caught doing something private.

---

The sign came down five weeks later. The new owners had a backlit plastic thing, blue, that said something he didn't bother to read.

But he'd asked for the old board, and the son had said yes, and now it leaned against the wall of Walt's garage, DOT'S DINER in fresh red over fifty years of older red, and every morning he went out with his coffee, black, in an ugly brown mug, and said good morning to it.

It never answered. That was fine. He knew what she'd say.
